Population-level separable treatment effects and tests

Source: R/effects.R
easte.Rd

Estimates the expected absolute separable treatment effects \(EASTE_{j,K} = E\{|STE_{j,K}(X)|\}\), their difference \(DEASTE_K = EASTE_{1,K} - EASTE_{2,K}\) and the average effects \(E\{STE_{j,K}(X)\}\) and \(E\{TTE_K(X)\}\), where the expectation is over a distribution of the covariates, with delta-method standard errors and a Wald test (Section 3.2.2 of the paper).

Usage

easte(
  object,
  newdata = NULL,
  y1 = NULL,
  y2 = NULL,
  K = NULL,
  alternative = c("less", "greater", "two.sided"),
  conf.level = 0.95,
  covariate_variance = is.null(newdata)
)

Arguments

object

A fitted model returned by biscal().

newdata

Optional data frame of covariate values over which the effects are averaged (see the section on the covariate distribution).

y1, y2

Thresholds of the generalized odds ratio: categories of the first and second response (any category except the highest). Default to the lowest category, the only choice for binary responses.

K

End time point(s): the visit(s) at which the effects are defined. Defaults to the last visit of the data; a vector gives effects at several visits (see plot.biscal_aste()). Visits after the last visit of the data are extrapolated with the fitted transition models (with a warning).

alternative

Alternative hypothesis for the test of \(DASTE_K\) (\(DEASTE_K\) for easte()): "less" (default, as in the paper), "greater" or "two.sided".

conf.level

Confidence level of the Wald intervals.

covariate_variance

Add the sampling variance of the covariates to the standard errors? Defaults to TRUE when the empirical distribution of the data is used (newdata = NULL) and FALSE otherwise.

Value

An object of class "biscal_easte", a list with components

effects

Data frame with one row per end time and effect (ESTE1, ESTE2, ETTE, EASTE1, EASTE2, DEASTE): estimate, std.error, conf.low, conf.high and mc_se.

test

Data frame with the test of \(DEASTE_K\): estimate, std.error, statistic (\(z\)) and p.value.

n_rows

Number of covariate rows averaged.

and the settings used.

Covariate distribution

The expectation is approximated by the average over the rows of newdata.

  • By default (newdata = NULL) these are the covariates of the subjects in the data (their empirical distribution). The standard errors then add the sampling variability of the covariates, \(\widehat{var}\{h(X)\}/n\), to the delta-method variance of the estimated coefficients.

  • Alternatively, newdata may hold a large number of draws from a model for the covariate distribution (in the paper, a Gaussian mixture for the continuous covariates within groups defined by the discrete ones), or the profiles of a target population. The standard errors then reflect the uncertainty in the estimated coefficients only, treating the covariate distribution as known, as in the authors' implementation; the column mc_se gives the Monte Carlo standard error of the average when the rows are independent draws.

Inference

Standard errors use the delta method (the variance formula following equation (27) of the paper), with central-difference derivatives of the average with respect to the coefficients, as in aste(). When the average is over the covariates of the subjects in the data (newdata = NULL), the sampling variance of the covariates is added (see covariate_variance). The paper models the covariate distribution parametrically, \(f_X(x; \alpha)\), and its variance formula also includes the uncertainty of the estimated \(\alpha\); when newdata holds draws from such a fitted model, that component is not included, as in the authors' implementation. The default test is that of the paper, \(H_0: DEASTE_K \ge 0\) against \(H_1: DEASTE_K < 0\), with p-value \(\Phi(z)\); confidence intervals are Wald intervals.

References

Hu, P. and Yi, G. Y. (2026). Inference about separable causal effects with longitudinal bivariate ordinal responses with missingness and censoring. Statistics in Medicine, 45, e70320. doi:10.1002/sim.70320

See also

aste() for effects given covariate values.

Examples

fit <- biscal(cbind(y1, y2) ~ x1 + x2, data = simtrial, id = "id",
              time = "visit", treatment = "trt")
easte(fit)
#> Separable treatment effects averaged over covariates (population level)
#> Average over 1000 rows of the covariates of the fitted data
#> Thresholds: y1 <= 0, y2 <= 0; Wald 95% confidence intervals
#> Standard errors include the sampling variability of the covariates
#> 
#> End time K = 10:
#>        Estimate Std. Error Lower 95% Upper 95%
#> ESTE1  -0.06862    0.02125   -0.1103  -0.02696
#> ESTE2  -0.04283    0.01739  -0.07691 -0.008757
#> ETTE   -0.05573    0.01040  -0.07612  -0.03534
#> EASTE1  0.06868    0.02122   0.02710    0.1103
#> EASTE2  0.04283    0.01739  0.008757   0.07691
#> DEASTE  0.02585    0.03276  -0.03835   0.09005
#> H0: DEASTE >= 0 vs H1: DEASTE < 0: z = 0.7892, p-value = 0.785

# averaging over draws from a model for the covariates instead
set.seed(1)
draws <- data.frame(x1 = rnorm(2000), x2 = rbinom(2000, 1, 0.4))
easte(fit, newdata = draws)
#> Separable treatment effects averaged over covariates (population level)
#> Average over 2000 rows of the supplied covariate values
#> Thresholds: y1 <= 0, y2 <= 0; Wald 95% confidence intervals
#> Standard errors exclude the sampling variability of the covariates
#> 
#> End time K = 10:
#>        Estimate Std. Error Lower 95% Upper 95%
#> ESTE1  -0.06764    0.02111   -0.1090  -0.02627
#> ESTE2  -0.04252    0.01726  -0.07635 -0.008702
#> ETTE   -0.05508    0.01033  -0.07533  -0.03484
#> EASTE1  0.06782    0.02099   0.02668    0.1090
#> EASTE2  0.04252    0.01726  0.008702   0.07635
#> DEASTE  0.02530    0.03245  -0.03831   0.08890
#> H0: DEASTE >= 0 vs H1: DEASTE < 0: z = 0.7795, p-value = 0.782
